title: PostgreSQL & Event-Driven Data Architecture
description: Master relational database optimization, EXPLAIN ANALYZE query tuning, GIN/B-Tree indexing, and event-driven data modeling.
body: A comprehensive database engineering track focusing on high-performance PostgreSQL query execution, indexing strategies, schema migrations, and event streaming integration.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: Database Normalization & Schema Design
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: The Anomalous Database
A developer stores user addresses as comma-separated text inside the `users` table. When a user updates their state, half the orders table breaks due to stale address strings.

### Relational Integrity (3NF)

Third Normal Form eliminates this class of bug by ensuring every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key — an address is its own entity, not a string glued onto `users`:

```sql
-- WRONG: denormalized, redundant, and inconsistent the moment one order's
-- copy of the address diverges from the user's current address
CREATE TABLE users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  address TEXT  -- "123 Main St, Springfield, IL" as one opaque string
);

-- RIGHT: addresses are a normalized entity referenced by foreign key
CREATE TABLE addresses (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  street TEXT NOT NULL,
  city TEXT NOT NULL,
  state TEXT NOT NULL,
  postal_code TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  current_address_id INT REFERENCES addresses(id)
);

-- An order captures a SNAPSHOT of the address at order time (a deliberate
-- denormalization for immutability, not an accidental one) — this is
-- different from the bug: it's an explicit historical record, versioned
-- by its own id, not a stale copy nobody intended to freeze.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT REFERENCES users(id),
  shipping_address_id INT REFERENCES addresses(id) NOT NULL
);
```

Updating a user's `current_address_id` now changes their address everywhere that references it live, while past orders keep pointing at the specific `addresses` row that was current when they were placed — correctness by construction, not by remembering to update every copy.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: The real lesson isn't "always normalize" — it's knowing WHICH duplication is a bug (the `users.address` string silently drifting from reality) versus WHICH duplication is an intentional design decision (an order's frozen shipping address snapshot). Foreign keys make the first kind of drift structurally impossible.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: EXPLAIN ANALYZE & Query Plan Breakdown
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: 10-Second API Spikes
Your analytics dashboard takes 12 seconds to load. You open PostgreSQL and run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`:
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM articles WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED' ORDER BY created_at DESC;
```

```text
Sort  (cost=98234.11..98484.11 rows=100000 width=612) (actual time=11890.2..11902.4 rows=98421 loops=1)
  Sort Key: created_at DESC
  Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 41280kB
  Buffers: shared read=2000000
  ->  Seq Scan on articles  (cost=0.00..64123.00 rows=100000 width=612)
                            (actual time=0.03..11450.88 rows=98421 loops=1)
        Filter: (status = 'PUBLISHED'::text)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 1901579
        Buffers: shared read=2000000
Planning Time: 0.089 ms
Execution Time: 11982.55 ms
```

You discover a `Seq Scan` reading 2,000,000 table pages from disk into memory on every single HTTP request — plus `Sort Method: external merge Disk: 41280kB`, meaning the sort itself spilled to disk because the full unfiltered result set doesn't fit in `work_mem`.

### Two Separate Problems in One Plan

| Symptom in the plan | Root cause | Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `Seq Scan` + `Rows Removed by Filter: 1901579` | No index supports `status = 'PUBLISHED'` | Add a targeted index (Lesson 1.3) |
| `Sort Method: external merge Disk: 41280kB` | Sorting happens AFTER the full table scan, on the unfiltered+unindexed result | An index on `(status, created_at)` lets PostgreSQL read rows already in sorted order — no separate sort step needed at all |

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: `Rows Removed by Filter` is the single most actionable number in this plan — it directly quantifies the wasted work: reading and then discarding 1.9 million rows to find 98,421 relevant ones. Any time this number is large relative to the rows actually returned, indexing the filter condition is the first thing to try.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Advanced Indexing: B-Tree, GIN, and Partial Indexes
lessons.body:
### The Solution: Targeted Indexing
Create a Partial B-Tree Index to dramatically reduce index memory footprint, matching BOTH the filter and the sort order from Lesson 1.2's query in a single index:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_published
ON articles (created_at DESC)
WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED';
```

```text
Index Scan using idx_articles_published on articles
  (cost=0.42..3421.18 rows=98421 width=612) (actual time=0.08..1.92 rows=98421 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=412
Planning Time: 0.071 ms
Execution Time: 2.14 ms
```

Query execution drops from 12,000ms to 2ms — because the index is both a filter (`WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED'`) AND a pre-sorted structure (`created_at DESC`), PostgreSQL no longer needs a separate `Seq Scan` step or a disk-spilling `Sort` step at all: it walks the index in the exact order the query needs and returns rows directly.

### When to Reach for GIN Instead

A B-Tree index like the one above only helps equality/range/sort queries. If `articles` also needs full-text search (`WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('postgres')`) or JSONB containment (`WHERE metadata @> '{"featured": true}'`), those operators need a **GIN** index instead — a B-Tree, no matter how well-tuned, has no code path for evaluating containment or full-text match operators.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: The 6,000x speedup here (12,000ms → 2ms) came from ONE index matching the query's exact filter and sort — not from tuning PostgreSQL's memory settings or adding hardware. Indexing the actual access pattern is almost always the highest-leverage fix available before reaching for infrastructure changes.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Data Modeling for Event Streams (CloudEvents)
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Microservice Coupling
Service A needs to notify Service B, C, and D whenever an order is placed. Direct REST calls mean Service A fails if any downstream service is slow or offline — and adding a fifth consumer means changing Service A's code yet again.

### The Event Streaming Solution: Publish, Don't Call

Instead of Service A calling B, C, and D directly, it publishes one immutable event; any number of consumers subscribe independently, and Service A never needs to know they exist:

```json
{
  "specversion": "1.0",
  "type": "com.geekgully.order.placed",
  "source": "/orders-service",
  "id": "a1b2c3d4-...",
  "time": "2026-09-21T14:03:11Z",
  "datacontenttype": "application/json",
  "data": {
    "order_id": "ord_9f8e7d",
    "customer_id": "cust_4a2b1c",
    "total_amount": 4999,
    "currency": "USD",
    "line_items": [
      {"sku": "WIDGET-100", "quantity": 2, "unit_price": 2499}
    ]
  }
}
```

```text
                              ┌──────────────────┐
                     ┌────────► Inventory Service │  reserves stock
                     │        └──────────────────┘
┌───────────────┐    │        ┌──────────────────┐
│ Orders Service │────┼────────► Billing Service   │  charges card
│ (publishes ONE │    │        └──────────────────┘
│  event)        │    │        ┌──────────────────┐
└───────────────┘    └────────► Notification Svc  │  sends confirmation email
                              └──────────────────┘
     order.placed event → Kafka topic "orders.events"
     Each consumer reads independently, at its own pace, with no
     coupling to whether the others succeed, are slow, or are offline.
```

The CloudEvents envelope (`specversion`, `type`, `source`, `id`, `time`) is a CNCF standard specifically so that consumers across different services and even different languages can parse the envelope uniformly, regardless of what's inside `data`.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: The immutability of the event matters as much as the decoupling — `order.placed` is a permanent fact about something that already happened, never edited after publication. A NEW event (`order.cancelled`) represents a later fact; nobody goes back and mutates the original `order.placed` record, which is what makes event streams safely replayable from the beginning of the log.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS)
Lesson 2.3: Knowledge Check — Data Architecture
lessons.body:
**Question 1:** In the normalization example, why is an order's `shipping_address_id` snapshot NOT the same kind of problem as the original `users.address` string bug?

A) They're the same problem and both should be fixed identically
B) The order's address is an intentional, explicit historical record tied to a specific point in time (when the order was placed), while the `users.address` string was an accidental duplicate expected to always reflect the CURRENT address — one is designed immutability, the other is unintentional drift
C) Foreign keys prevent all duplication automatically
D) Orders don't actually need addresses at all

**Correct answer: B.** Normalization isn't about eliminating all duplication everywhere — it's about eliminating duplication that should stay in sync but doesn't. A deliberately frozen historical snapshot, referenced by its own stable foreign key, is a correct design choice.

---

**Question 2:** Why did adding `idx_articles_published` eliminate BOTH the sequential scan AND the disk-spilling sort in the EXPLAIN plan?

A) Indexes only ever fix scans, never sorts
B) The index was built on `(created_at DESC) WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED'` — it simultaneously satisfies the filter (only published rows are in the index) and the sort order (entries are already stored in descending created_at order), so PostgreSQL can walk it directly with no separate scan or sort step
C) PostgreSQL automatically rewrites all sequential scans into index scans regardless of the index definition
D) It only fixed the scan; the sort still spills to disk

**Correct answer: B.** An index's column order and direction can double as a pre-computed sort — when a query's `ORDER BY` matches an index's stored order, PostgreSQL can skip the sort step entirely.

---

**Question 3:** What consistency tradeoff does CQRS deliberately accept, and why is it acceptable for an analytics dashboard but NOT for an inventory count that must never oversell?

A) CQRS has no consistency tradeoffs
B) The read-side projection is eventually consistent — updated asynchronously after the write commits — which is fine for a dashboard where being a few seconds stale is harmless, but unacceptable for inventory where a stale read could let two customers both "successfully" buy the last unit
C) CQRS makes writes eventually consistent, not reads
D) The tradeoff only applies to Elasticsearch, not other read stores

**Correct answer: B.** Eventual consistency on the read side is the core CQRS tradeoff — appropriate when a brief staleness window is harmless, wrong when the read result directly gates a decision (like allowing a purchase) that requires strict, immediate consistency.
